title: Geometric clocks on causal graphs
html: Marzke–Wheeler axiomatic relativity and geometric clocks for causal graphs generated by hypergraph rewriting, and the set-theoretic structure that connects them to the rewriting systems.

title: Insertion Lie brackets for hypergraphs
html: Lie and Poisson structures on hypergraphs, towards a Hamiltonian formalism for hypergraph rewriting.

title: Discrete difference operators on graphs
html: Discrete analogues of differential operators on graphs and hypergraphs, the starting point for several further developments in discrete differential geometry.

title: Emergent Geometry
html: Which smooth geometries can arise as infrageometric limits of graphs generated by given rules? We study scaled Gromov–Hausdorff convergence of metric-measure spaces with specified coarse-graining maps, and ask when minimal models of geometric objects and their observables converge to smooth geometric structures and their corresponding observables. This includes weak convergence of the measures associated with vertex and edge densities of multiobjects to measures on limiting geometric objects. How does convergence depend on the rules and observer scale? What is the landscape of possible geometric limits for a given class of rules? Can we explain the emergence of linearity, Riemannian geometry, and symplectic geometry? Under what conditions do discrete constructions whose smooth counterparts agree approach the same result, such as dimension estimates from ball volumes and shell sizes or different constructions of scalar products? At finite observer scales, which smooth geometries best approximate the graph, and how can distance measurements, volume growth, curvature bounds, and topology constrain the possibilities?

title: Emergent Spacetime
html: How does spacetime emerge from hypergraph rewriting models for given observers? We study a single rewriting history through its causal structure, starting with a chosen observer chain and foliation. Nearby observer chains intersect the foliation to represent germs based at the original observer. From these data, we seek spatial slices fibered over ℤ³, with gauge degrees of freedom in the fibers and coarse-graining maps between descriptions at different observer scales. How does spatial connectivity arise from causal relations, and how do objects persist between successive slices? How do the resulting descriptions depend on the observer chain, foliation, and nearby chains? Can different observers obtain compatible descriptions of the same rewriting history? We aim to make the construction explicit and identify the conditions under which spatial, temporal, and gauge structures arise.

title: InfraEconomics
html: What are the simplest computational models that exhibit economic phenomena? Following the approach of infrageometry, we explore two directions. In one direction, we ask whether observable economic behavior can emerge from simple systems with resource constraints and local interactions. For example, consider a cellular automaton with an additional rule: whenever the number of black cells exceeds 20, five black cells in the densest region turn white. How does this constraint affect the automaton’s behavior, and how does it recover after these disaster events? Does deleting cells in the densest region have different consequences from deleting them randomly? Which observables have a meaningful economic interpretation, and how do their patterns vary across families of cellular automata? The other infra-direction represents economic states as hypergraphs and economic processes, such as production, exchange, and consumption, as elementary rewriting rules. Can these models recover familiar economic curves, and under what assumptions? Which minimal mechanisms determine stability, shortages, and recovery after disruption?
